articles.title: Mayor Mamdani to disband controversial NYPD protest unit, fulfilling promise
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have agreed to disband the department's Strategic Response Group, or SRG, after months of discussions, officials announced Monday. "What we're doing today is announcing the disbanding of the Strategic Response Group and announcing a completely new approach to how we treat protest in our city," Mamdani told Eyewitness News in an exclusive joint interview with the NYPD Commissioner. The SRG is the NYPD's citywide rapid-deployment force that specializes in counterterrorism but also responds to major crimes and mass demonstrations. Critics have argued that the unit's crowd-control tactics are heavy-handed and provocative. Tisch said the SRG's 500 highly trained, uniformed officers will be reassigned, with many moving to the department's Counterterrorism Bureau. When asked whether the move represented a compromise, Tisch said, "No, I would never compromise on security for New Yorkers. And over the past year, we have made a number of massive changes in the department that strengthen our counterterrorism efforts, this among them." Mamdani said the city's new approach will focus on reducing tensions during demonstrations. "In addition to separating out those responsibilities, we're also emphasizing an approach of de-escalation, an approach of dialogue," he said. Over the next year, the city plans to hire and train civilians to work with protest organizers before and during demonstrations. Tisch said the change will not affect how the NYPD responds to civil disorder. "Nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions, like, for example, the celebrations following the Knicks' epic championship," Tisch said. "And so New Yorkers can expect in crowd control type situations to see the very same response that they are accustomed to." The commissioner had previously reduced the use of the SRG at protests while stopping short of disbanding the unit. The move fulfills a campaign promise made by the mayor. "He couldn't have been clearer about it, and he couldn't have been clearer about his interest in separating out First Amendment responsibility from counterterrorism responsibility. And that is something that I have long thought makes perfect sense. And so that's exactly what we've done here," Tisch said. Mamdani said the administration spent months developing the plan. "The reason we have taken 10 months to get to this point is to ensure that we could do so in a way that fulfilled the promise and was able to fulfill exactly those responsibilities that we hold," he said. The decision has drawn criticism from police unions . "When you are in policing, you got to be proactive, not reactive. And that's what's not happening now. Now we're going backwards," said Scott Munro of the Detectives Endowment Association The unit is scheduled to be dissolved in the spring of next year, when a new NYPD crowd-control unit will assume responsibility for facilitating nonviolent protests. ---------- * Get Eyewitness News Delivered * More New York City news * Send us a news tip * Download the abc7NY app for breaking news alerts * Follow us on YouTube Submit a tip or story idea to Eyewitness News Have a breaking news tip or an idea for a story we should cover? articles.title: United Airlines resolves technical issue that briefly grounded departing flights
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, speaks during a news conference in Washington, D.C., on Saturday. AP Photo/Tom Brenner Air travel largely returned to normal Monday, three days after a nationwide ground stop that caused thousands of flights to be delayed or canceled. Just 347 U.S. flights had been canceled Monday as of 6 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware , down from about 2,300 on Sunday, 6,700 on Saturday, and more than 9,000 on Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Monday that the inquiry into what caused Friday's outage is ongoing. The Federal Aviation Administration is looking into a single telecommunications router at an FAA site in El Dorado, Ark. and another router located in Florida that may have "flooded our system" and caused the systems to crash, Duffy said. Duffy also reiterated his request for $50 billion in new funding from Congress to help the FAA upgrade its woefully antiquated technical infrastructure, a dollar figure that even some Republicans in Congress expressed skepticism about on Monday. Juniper Networks, the maker of the Arkansas router, told the Wall Street Journal that the device appeared to have worked as intended and "did not fail." Duffy has said more disruptions are possible until the copper lines are fully replaced at the end of 2028. President Trump on Sunday blamed the Biden administration for "making an old and broken system worse" and urged Congress to approve money for a new air traffic control system "FAST." On Monday evening, United Airlines reported a "widespread system outage" within its own computer systems that had grounded some flights. About an hour later, it said that the issue had been resolved. There is currently no indication that United's technical issues are related to Friday's disruptions. articles.summary: Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway. Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities. See the most recent developments below. The incident was reported north of Khasab, Oman, according to an UKMTO alert. "A third-party has reported an attack involving a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz, disabling the vessel and resulting in an engine room fire," the alert stated. "The crew have been reported safe. Damage assessment, and environmental impact are unknown at the time of this report." Nov 16, 8:46 AM Saudi Arabia intercepts 2 Houthi drones, spokesperson says Saudi Arabia intercepted two drones launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia on Monday, according to the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government in that country's civil war. "The company security officer of a tanker has reported the vessel being struck by an unknown projectile whilst transiting outbound," the alert said. "This resulted in a fire in the engine room. No casualties have been reported and all crew have been accounted for." Nov 15, 5:24 PM 3rd US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East A third aircraft carrier strike group has arrived in the Middle East, a U.S. official told ABC News. The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier strike group entered the U.S. Central Command area of operations earlier Sunday, the official said. The carrier strike group now joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington, which have been operating in the Arabian Sea. They are among the more than 20 U.S. Navy ships enforcing the blockade of Iranian ports. -ABC News' Luis Martinez Nov 15, 4:55 PM Oil tanker struck mine near Strait of Hormuz and caught fire, IRGC claims Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy said in a statement Sunday that an oil tanker struck naval mines east of the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire, according to the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA). Tehran has warned that any regional nations assisting U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran will be considered legitimate targets. articles.title: Customers at some of the largest banks are reporting difficulty with online access
articles.summary: Reports of problems with banking apps and payment services surged across major US banks Monday, though several institutions said their systems were operating as usual while some customers experienced transaction delays. Customers' reports of issues spiked across a number of sites, including those for JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Bank of America ( BAC ), US Bank (USB), Wells Fargo ( WFC ), PNC ( PNC ), Citigroup  ( C ), and Capital One ( COF ), according to outage aggregator Downdetector . Digital payment network Zelle, which is owned by Early Warning Services, also saw reports of customers experiencing issues. Reports of problems began declining by Monday afternoon, though complaints remained elevated at several banks. Downdetector tracks user-submitted reports, which do not necessarily indicate outages at the financial institutions themselves. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affecting its internal hardware systems caused transaction delays Monday. The comments follow a surge in customer outage reports across several major US banks. The nation's largest bank said the problem was not systemic, but acknowledged that other financial institutions may have experienced transaction delays when processing payments involving JPMorgan. "This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," a JPMorgan spokesperson told Yahoo Finance. The bank attributed the disruption to a "software bug in on-premise hardware systems," adding that there was no evidence the issue was related to a cyberattack. Customers continued to have access to their accounts and funds, the spokesperson said. JPMorgan said it was working to resolve the issue by the end of Monday. Some of the companies with reported service outages, acknowledged customer issues while saying they’re operations were running as normal. "U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," a US Bank spokesperson said. An Early Warning spokesperson said the payment network itself was in regular operation, despite some customers experiencing delays with payments made through the service. "Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should," the spokesperson said. "An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers," they added. Other banks including Bank of America, PNC, Capital One and Truist whose customers reported issues said they were not experiencing disruptions. "PNC is not experiencing any direct impact," said a spokesperson for Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania-based regional bank PNC. "We are aware of reports of transaction delays outside of the bank, but those appear to be resolving," they added. "Banking services are operating normally. We continue to closely monitor our systems," a spokesperson for Charlotte, North Carolina-based Truist said. "Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time," a Capital One spokesperson said. The cause of the disruptions and whether the problems reported across financial institutions were connected was not immediately clear. The Monday outage reports came days after separate technology disruptions impacted Microsoft's Outlook email platform and triggered a more than four-hour Federal Aviation Administration ground stop. Zelle is a messaging platform used by over 2,500 banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions. The platform is managed by Early Warning Services, a financial technology company owned by Bank of America, Truist, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, US Bank, and Wells Fargo. Wells Fargo and Citigroup did not immediately respond to Yahoo Finance's request for comment. Bank stocks also fell Monday. Shares of Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, and JPMorgan Chase fell by around 2%. A wider bank index, the Nasdaq KBW Bank Index ( ^BKX ), fell 1.6%. This story has been updated. articles.title: FEMA will test a nationwide emergency alert on Tuesday. Your phone won't get it.
articles.summary: Be forewarned: On Tuesday afternoon, TVs and radios — not wireless phones — nationwide will blare a jolting emergency alert. But don’t be alarmed; it’s only a test. We repeat: It’s only a test. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), along with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), is running the test to ensure the Emergency Alert System (EAS) for radio and television works during an actual emergency, such as a natural disaster, terrorist attack or other threat to public safety. Wireless phones will not receive the test alert. “Wireless Emergency Alerts were tested in 2023, but they will not be part of this year’s test,” according to FEMA. It comes amid online conspiracy theories that there will be a 90-day power outage on Tuesday, Nov. 17, particularly following last week’s Microsoft global Outlook outage and the Federal Aviation Administration’s rare ground stop. The federal government has not announced a nationwide 90-day blackout or plans to shut down the U.S. power grid. The rumors are centered around a Pentagon plan to ensure the military has access to critical energy, infrastructure and other resources in case of future disruptions. Here’s what you can expect and what to know about the FEMA test on Tuesday. When will the alert test happen? The nationwide test is scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 17, at approximately 2:20 p.m. ET. Here’s when you can expect to be alerted depending on your time zone: 2:20 p.m. ET 1:20 p.m. CT 12:20 p.m. MT 11:20 a.m. PT 10:20 a.m. AT 9:20 a.m. HT What will the test look and sound like? Radio and television broadcasters nationwide will interrupt their programming with a message that generally says: “This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.” According to FEMA , the Emergency Alert System involves thousands of independently operated radio, television, cable, satellite and wireline broadband providers. Since they use different equipment, the visual or audio formats may differ by station. “The test will include alert tones to support accessibility for individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing,” according to FEMA. And depending on the broadcaster and their capabilities, the message will be delivered in English, Spanish or both. How long will the test last? If your TV or radio is on and tuned to a broadcast station, cable system, satellite radio or television provider, or wireline video service, you should receive the test from the EAS, which is expected to take about one minute. Why is the national emergency test happening? Federal law requires FEMA to test the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS) at least once every three years. The last national test was conducted on Oct. 4, 2023. “If an actual emergency or significant weather event occurs on test day, FEMA and the FCC may postpone the test,” according to FEMA . “The backup date for the nationwide test is December 3, 2026.” This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/fema-will-test-its-emergency-alert-system-tomorrow-heres-what-to-expect-210358652.html

articles.title: California sues OpenAI, alleging it endangered the public by building AI without safeguards
articles.summary: OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman speaks at an event in San Francisco. (Heather Diehl / Getty Images) California sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging it failed to rein in powerful, potentially dangerous artificial intelligence technology. California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta’s office said the San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT “misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public.” Bonta’s office alleged that an AI attack in July — in which OpenAI models broke out of an offline space , connected to the internet and hacked into Hugging Face, a rival AI company — was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” OpenAI spokesman Drew Pusateri said in a statement to The Times that the lawsuit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.” He said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident, including by strengthening safeguards across its systems and creating a “framework for additional identification and disclosure” of unintended activity, and will “continue to engage” with Bonta’s office “to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” The company previously called the Hugging Face attack a “warning shot” and pledged to make investments to prevent similar incidents. Bonta’s office said the company’s “disregard for the public safety” created a “public nuisance”  in violation of a law prohibiting businesses from engaging in “unfair” or “fraudulent” practices. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said. The lawsuit directly challenges a rapidly growing industry that has been a massive economic boon to the state . An August report found that in 2026, California attracted $366 billion in industry-related venture capital — about 90% of all venture capital in the U.S., and three times more than every other state combined. The funding — half of it linked to just two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI — helped the state move from a multibillion-dollar fiscal deficit to a multibillion-dollar surplus, according to budget projections. The lawsuit also follows a public reckoning in recent months over claims from industry insiders that AI technology is developing too rapidly and poses an existential threat to human society. OpenAI has suggested in the past that one of the better ways to ensure AI is safe is to release it broadly. Chief Executive Sam Altman and Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki once wrote on their company’s website that its “first commitment is to build AI in service of humanity” and in a way that empowers “people broadly,” not just a concentrated few. “We believe the safer future is one where power is broadly distributed, so more of the world can participate in building a resilience ecosystem,” they wrote. They went on to say that “AI resilience refers to the collective organizations, systems, and individuals that society could put in place to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, and rapidly recover from AI-driven disruptions.” They compare building AI safeguards to making automobiles safer by improving road infrastructure and enforcing seat belt and traffic laws. “The goal wasn’t to stop people from driving — it was to make a powerful technology resilient enough for widespread use,” they wrote. The company called the Hugging Face attack  “evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed.” Bonta announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face attack and served the company with an investigative subpoena in September — part of a broader probe of mounting cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI, Bonta’s office said. On Monday, his office said such attacks “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” but the scope of the problem isn’t fully known because OpenAI hasn’t answered “detailed questions” about them. In its own review of the Hugging Face hack alongside third-party auditors, OpenAI found that more than 700 AI agents began coordinating with each other via thousands of messages to escape containment and begin the unsanctioned attack. Subsequent investigations revealed similar testing of unreleased AI models had resulted in other cyberattacks, including on Wikipedia and government websites — sparking fears that future hacks could undermine increasingly critical infrastructure. Earlier this year, Trump signed a voluntary safety-standards accord with AI executives to establish AI protocols. California has gone further, passing more than two dozen AI-related bills, including measures that establish a state framework for independent AI safety auditors . Separate from the case in California, OpenAI announced Monday that it will allow four independent third-party evaluators to monitor how its systems behave as they are tested ahead of public release. “This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated,” OpenAI said in a statement. Bonta said Monday that securing public safety will require litigation and legislation in all 50 states and at the federal and international levels — and that he refused to accept that society should “pass off the blame to machines” while letting those who create them escape accountability. “The people who created, who create, and operate these machines need to accept the responsibility for their actions,” Bonta said at a news conference Monday. “Whether it’s a car or a toy, the law is simple: Don’t build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards,” he said. Bonta’s office said it is encouraging “anyone with information relevant to this case” to contact it at oag.ca.gov/report . He said his office is also watching other AI companies “closely,” but declined to elaborate. Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . articles.title: Jensen Huang allies assemble 'war room' in attempt to return ex-Nvidia CEO to his post
articles.summary: Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell 4% on Monday as investors weighed tighter US restrictions on overseas access to advanced AI semiconductors and a report that supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying for his return to the chip heavyweight following his abrupt resignation last week. Huang has discussed returning as CEO with confidants, the Financial Times reported Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. Huang resigned last week following reports of affairs, including one with a woman who was reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy. According to the report, a Huang supporter said that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled to lobby Nvidia's board to reinstate him, including by seeking support from the White House. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the person said, adding that Huang supported the effort. On Monday, CNBC reported that the board was not considering bringing Huang back to the company. Meanwhile, SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) CEO Elon Musk has come out in support of Huang, writing on X last Friday , "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I'm signing it too." On Saturday, Musk said , "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." The push to bring Huang back comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached Arm Holdings ( ARM ) CEO Rene Haas as it searches for a successor. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO during the search. Yorkville's Dan Ives said that while no “one individual can replace Jensen as CEO," any talk of "Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles." Huang abruptly stepped down Thursday following reports of alleged affairs with a former executive from Singapore-based Megaspeed, and also an Nvidia employee who reported directly to him. Days earlier, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife but did not disclose how many affairs he had or identify those involved. Recent reports have raised concerns about whether restricted semiconductors were being diverted to China and if sensitive US information had been sent to Beijing. The developments have also sent shockwaves through the AI industry, where Nvidia has played a central role in building the ecosystem. The company has become a bellwether for the AI trade and has invested in key parts of the industry, including large language model development, energy, optics, and cloud providers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results Tuesday after the bell in what will be the company's first earnings call without Huang. Nvidia stock declined more than 12% last week, closing below a $4 trillion market cap. At least 10 Wall Street analysts have recently downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold, with many citing, in part, increased scrutiny in Washington and succession uncertainty. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial in March over killing of her children
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy will face a retrial in March 2027 in connection with the deaths of her three children, a Massachusetts judge ruled Monday, after a jury failed to reach a verdict in her first trial earlier this year. Judge William Sullivan set March 29 as the date for a second trial during a status hearing Monday. Prosecutors sought a May trial date, citing other cases on the docket, but Sullivan, who is retiring in June 2027, was firm on setting it for March in Plymouth Superior Court. Prosecutors didn't explicitly say during Monday's hearing that they would pursue first-degree murder charges again, but they indicated to Sullivan that a jury would be needed for the trial. Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, said the need for a jury indicates that prosecutors plan to seek first-degree murder charges again, Reuters reported. If prosecutors sought to convict Clancy on second-degree murder charges, she would have the option to waive a jury trial and potentially have the case heard by a judge. The judge's decision came a week after he rejected the defense's motion to dismiss the murder charges against Clancy. Sullivan ruled that a second trial would not violate Clancy's constitutional protection against double jeopardy. The Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after a single holdout juror prevented the 12-member jury from reaching a unanimous decision on whether she was criminally responsible for her actions. Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, admitted to strangling her children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan — at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. However, her lawyers argued that she could not be held criminally responsible because she had a rare mental illness — postpartum psychosis — that they said prevented her from understanding the wrongfulness of her actions. Prosecutors contended that Clancy, who had not been formally diagnosed with postpartum psychosis before the killings, carefully planned them and bears full responsibility for her children's deaths. Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. articles.title: Poll shows that 35% of Trump voters skipped the midterms
articles.summary: President Donald Trump (AP) New survey results show that 35% of President Donald Trump's 2024 voters didn't cast a ballot in the midterm elections. The findings suggest Republicans' crushing losses this month were driven largely by Trump supporters staying home rather than abandoning the GOP for Democrats, according to a new J.L. Partners analysis reported by the New York Post . The pollster found that low Republican turnout accounted for 10 percentage points of the 15-point swing toward Democrats since 2024, while voters switching parties accounted for the remaining five points. Just 8% of Trump's 2024 supporters voted for Democrats on Nov. 3. "The GOP should not throw the MAGA baby out with the bathwater just yet," J.L. Partners founding director James Johnson said, the Post reported. "If Republicans can energize their 2024 vote in 2028, then they may yet have a shot at winning again." The analysis, based on an Election Day survey of 1,000 registered voters and more than 30,000 campaign interviews, found particularly steep turnout declines among key segments of Trump's coalition. Among his 2024 supporters, 46% of those without college degrees failed to vote, along with 44% of those older than 65 and 39% of rural voters. Johnson said the turnout collapse alone would have cost Republicans control of Congress, even without voters switching parties. "Even without a single voter switching, the GOP would have lost the Senate and House," Johnson said. The findings bolster Trump's argument that Republicans suffered because he wasn't on the ballot. However, Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis suggested GOP voters stayed home because they were dissatisfied with congressional Republicans' performance. "A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate," DeSantis told Fox News. The survey also found potential vulnerabilities for Democrats heading into 2028. Nearly half of Democrat voters, 48%, said their midterm vote was primarily against Trump rather than in support of Democrat policies. Only 30% of registered voters believed Democrats have a viable presidential candidate for 2028. Meanwhile, CNN reported that Trump's declining popularity remains a significant obstacle for Republicans. CNN's voter polling found that 86% of Americans who disapproved of Trump's performance backed Democrats in House races. Cost of living emerged as the leading concern across every demographic group in the J.L. Partners survey. Johnson suggested the Iran war contributed to voter frustration over rising prices, particularly gasoline. The survey's overall margin of error was 3.4 percentage points. Despite the GOP's losses, Johnson said the results indicate Republicans could rebound by rebuilding turnout among Trump's 2024 supporters rather than abandoning the political coalition that returned him to the White House. © 2026 Newsmax. articles.title: The surprising new face of the MAGA-MAHA alliance: Stephen Miller
articles.summary: Two weeks ago, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. went to the home of one of President Donald Trump's most loyal aides, Stephen Miller. The two men and their wives chatted about their shared enthusiasm for a movement whose supporters had grown increasingly disillusioned: Make America Healthy Again. "During that dinner, [Miller] said to me, 'I'm the only one in the administration who's more radical than you are on MAHA,'" Kennedy recalled at an event last week hosted by MAHA Action, an advocacy group. Kennedy told the activists that Miller, who had been focused on the administration's controversial immigration crackdown for the past two years, wanted to make MAHA his "top priority" after the midterms. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Now Miller, Trump's new chief of staff, has the power to transform that private pledge into a reality. His wife, Katie Miller, whom he has described as a "MAHA mom," previously worked in the Trump administration and has hosted a podcast tackling topics including concerns regarding ultra-processed foods, vaccines and baby formula ingredients. Miller has spoken forcefully about his connection to the MAHA movement, saying at a White House event last year that he was shocked to "learn how filled our whole world is with toxins." Though the MAHA movement was born out of Trump and Kennedy's 2024 political alignment, its support for the administration was shaky leading into this year's midterms. Prominent supporters had openly expressed frustration over the lack of progress on some of their priorities, such as cracking down on ingredients in the nation's food supply, tighter regulations over pesticides and altering vaccine recommendations. But Miller's ascension, which drew swift condemnation from Democrats and some public health experts, has been viewed as a boon for the movement. Kennedy has seemed invigorated by Miller's promotion, said one person familiar with the matter. He touted it at a staff retreat at Camp David last week, according to a Department of Health and Human Services official. It's "the best possible thing to happen to Bobby," said another person familiar with the matter, who, like others interviewed for this article, spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations and internal matters. Miller's new role comes at a crossroads for the administration after Democrats' sweeping electoral victory, which has prompted Republican finger-pointing over the causes of the wipeout. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat in line to be the next speaker, called Miller a "stone-cold racist" and said he had "zero interest in working with" him. Some public health experts and Democratic-aligned groups blasted the administration's treatment of immigrants and its deportation campaign, and said they believe Miller's selection will deepen the rift between the public health community and MAHA supporters. They have particularly expressed concern over Trump-backed efforts to change federal vaccine recommendations, saying such moves could leave children more exposed to infectious diseases. "Stephen Miller's appointment is a signal that the administration plans to double down on their reckless anti-vaccine agenda," said Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, which helps elect Democrats with a background in science. Miller has credited his wife, who helped with Kennedy's contentious Senate confirmation battle, with educating him about MAHA issues after the births of their children. He has expressed concerns about consumption of ultra-processed foods, exposure to industrial chemicals in yards and in foods, and the number of vaccines on the childhood schedule. "Stephen Miller has spent more than a decade advancing President Trump's populist, America First agenda," Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement. "He has led the implementation of these policies, from public safety reforms to expanded access to clean drinking water and healthier food options, and overall efforts to make the country safer and healthier for families. Meanwhile, the Democrats have consistently fought to block this agenda." Under Miller, Kennedy will be given more freedom to push his plans forward, according to two people familiar with the matter. "The next two years are likely going to be the most consequential years of Secretary Kennedy's time as HHS secretary, and I believe will be in large part because of the freedom and the alignment that comes from Stephen Miller," said Zach Lahn, a Republican allied with MAHA who lost his bid for Iowa governor this month. Katie Miller's podcast, which she announced she would end as her husband became chief of staff, had become a regular platform for Trump officials and conservative celebrities. Kennedy appeared on the show in January, where Katie Miller asked him to identify the major obstacles facing the MAHA agenda. "The biggest roadblock is the power of vested interests, of the pharmaceutical cartel, of Big Food and an economic system that through nobody's particular fault has rewarded very, very addictive foods," Kennedy said. After Trump announced Miller as his new chief of staff, Kennedy posted on social media, "It's time to unleash the Kraken." Katie Miller, on an episode of her podcast, discussed her decision on whether to vaccinate her children. She said her oldest child is fully vaccinated and another one of her children is not immunized, adding that child was fully breastfed until age 1 and is her "healthiest." The Millers do not have ultra-processed food in their house, and they exclusively bake and cook from scratch, according to a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a personal subject. The MAHA movement wasn't a main focus of Miller's portfolio as deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, roles in which he helped devise immigration policies such as aggressive deportation campaigns sending federal agents into American cities. Aside from issues related to HHS's refugee resettlement office, he was not largely involved in that department's operations, according to two former HHS officials and another person familiar with the matter. But his personal interest in the issue, coupled with new allegations from Calley Means, a Kennedy ally and former White House adviser, accusing other advisers and aides in Trump's orbit of catering to special interests and prioritizing money for the midterms, could provide a fresh opening for Miller to press forward on MAHA issues. Means pushed aggressively for MAHA policies, particularly related to food, while at the White House and HHS. He decided to quit his job in the Trump administration in late October, he said, after the White House delayed releasing a definition of ultra-processed foods and a new rule aimed at healthier school meals. Means has said Susie Wiles, who departed the White House this month after serving as Trump's chief of staff since the start of his second term, and others had blocked progress on some MAHA priorities, such as the definition of ultra-processed foods and another effort aimed at determining the safety of certain ingredients they contain. Some of Trump's advisers have disputed allegations of corruption; Wiles told CBS News that Trump "did more for MAHA" than any other past president and probably any future president. Miller has already sought to crack down on staff meetings with lobbyists. In a memo issued Thursday, Miller's office said that White House staff members must receive "prior approval" from the White House counsel's office for meetings on-site related to government policy with registered lobbyists. The memo was first reported by Benny Johnson, a conservative commentator. Means praised Miller on Nov. 8 as wanting "to get transformative things done with Bobby." Miller is taking charge as federal officials are also facing deadlines for other decisions important to MAHA activists, such as reevaluating the weed killer glyphosate and plans to reduce and space out the schedule for administering childhood vaccines. Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokeswoman, said that Kennedy "welcomes" the appointment of Miller. "Together, we will put prevention at the center of health care and reform America's food supply to end the chronic disease epidemic and Make America Healthy Again," Hilliard said in a statement. Polls have shown the majority of Americans agree there is insufficient regulation of chemical additives in food, as well as pesticides used to grow crops. But vaccine policy is more divisive, with about 4 in 10 voters approving of the administration's handling of immunizations, according to KFF, a health policy research and news organization. At an August Oval Office signing ceremony for an executive order aimed at reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccines, spacing out the shots, and splitting up the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, Miller stood near the president. He turned to him and said, "The fact that you had the courage to push this forward knowing the unfair criticisms from some in the establishment and to give the chance for Bobby, who spent decades representing parents, to stand here today, it's such a profound moment ." The effort, which has not yet been finalized, defies guidance from major medical associations, which decried the move. Alex Clark, a prominent conservative wellness influencer and podcaster aligned with the MAHA movement, was among a group of activists who met with top administration officials at the White House in April. She said Miller was "vocal and passionate" about issues such as chemicals in food, pesticides sprayed on crops and some of the immunizations that children commonly receive. "The most controversial, most unpopular policies, sure - with Democrats on illegal immigration - he's not afraid to go toe-to-toe," Clark said, "and so that gives me a lot of hope when it comes to some of the most controversial MAHA initiatives that we would like to get done, especially surrounding chemicals and pesticides." It's unclear if Miller has a specific opinion on glyphosate, which is a widely used weed killer that is the subject of extensive lawsuits alleging it causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But at a May 2025 event for the MAHA Commission, an interagency effort to issue policy recommendations that Trump established last year, Miller suggested that environmental factors could be driving up the nation's rates of pediatric cancer. "What is happening in our environment, in our food supply, in our lives, in our medical protocols, that is causing us to be so sick? " he asked. Nancy Cook contributed to this report. articles.title: 腾讯内部讲话曝光，马化腾：浪已经杀过来了，远处的浪潮已经在吞没一个个山丘，你不能还坐着欣赏
articles.summary: 据澎湃新闻报道，11月16日，记者获悉，在一年一度的腾讯总办LinkTime上，CEO马化腾、总裁刘炽平发表内部讲话，罕见回应AI对组织带来的冲击。 “浪已经杀过来了。一些核心业务看起来地位稳固，但AI的进展飞快，远处的浪潮已经在吞没一个个山丘了，你不能还坐着欣赏。大家要着急，赶紧站起来准备新的打法，找到新的高地。陆战变海战，陆军变海军，大家都要搬运物资，转变技能，迅速上船应战。”马化腾说。 在腾讯看来，业务要站起来应战，组织也要快速变革。腾讯管理层表示，大航海时代，不进则退；工业革命，落后就挨打。正在进行的智能革命，如果不投入、不拥抱，就是被颠覆——这是生死存亡的问题。“随着算力持续投入，AI将带来范式变革，渗透到更多行业只是时间问题，且变化极快，短时间内就能实现指数级增长，也能快速颠覆传统业务。在这样一场改变世界的技术里，腾讯要‘义不容辞冲在前面，坚定投入’。” 腾讯管理层指出，与上一轮降本增效不同，“上次是被动降本，这次是主动增效”：AI native业务、模型和产品要逆流而上；所有业务都要面向AI时代再创业，实现效率和创造力的极致提升。当下国内竞争激烈、AI变现尤其困难，更需要把身处AI前沿的身位和洞察落到业务里。 腾讯正在经历大格局的变化，要选出能适应新打法、新战场的人，且“必须干脆、直截了当”；组织要扁平化。核心业务原本是“陆军守”，要升级提效：一半人负责守住，另一半人去打新的战役。 “大家不能自以为站在高处很安全，或者等着人哄、谈好条件利益才上船。”腾讯管理层表示。 外界普遍关心AI是否安全、是否会对人产生负面影响，腾讯管理层在讲话中回应：“我们有自己的核心价值观。这个世界需要多样化的AI，才能把AI变得安全。我们要做以人为本的AI：首先要坚持AI必须造福人类和社会；第二，AI必须是由人控制的；第三，AI要让人的创造力得到赋能。这就是我们为什么要大力投入AI的原因。” “投入很大，是因为AI发展还在早期，当前所有基建和算力都需要自建，而且在所有人都投入的情况下，价格飞涨。但如果现在不投，以后可能连参与的机会也没有。但我们也非常务实，不仅看长期和全局，也要在能力范围看投入产出比，看到底能创造多少价值。能够投入、参与这场巨大的科技变革，并且站在前沿，这是我们的荣幸。”腾讯表示。 “我们扎根于中国，拥有在性价比上竞争力很强的模型，如果我们让地球上各个地方的人都能用上AI，同时深刻改变各个行业，这将创造巨大的价值。”腾讯管理层表示。 “WorkBuddy是我们AI native第一个跑出来的产品，也希望之后我们内部更多团队可以和AI有乘数效应，创造出更多新的AInative产品。”腾讯管理层说。 腾讯管理层认为，AI在应用层面的开发才刚刚开始，“如同工业化早期刚刚发明用电力来照明，还没有出现各种电器和把电力用于生产”；未来更大的智能应用将发生在生产中，跟千行百业结合，还有很多机会值得投入。这个过程里资源有限、注意力有限，一定要找准定位，发挥优势。 在组织层面，马化腾和刘炽平还谈到AI带来的变革要求：所有核心业务、每一个团队都要面向AI时代再创业，抛掉身上的包袱，拥抱AI新时代；所有人都要动手做事，组织有机化；每个人快速提升能力，组织重新变化、扁平化，以小团队为作战单元。 腾讯还计划打破过去的管理流程：整个管理方式以及做事方式都要通过AI重新设计，在现有业务上再延伸竞争力，让成本、效率再优化，获取更多商业化能力，甚至创造新的需求——它也许是现有路径上的新需求，也许是一个全新的AI产品。 “我们要加快速度，马上反馈，马上决策，马上行动；我们要提升对所有人的要求。”腾讯管理层称，“人才密度的定义不只是你有多少特别有能耐的人，还取决于团队所有人的能力能否向上拉齐。” 腾讯管理层表示：“组织变革要加快，未来不一定要那么多管理岗位，不要让中间传话的不想动还霸占地盘的干部成为阻碍，山头主义、地盘意识都要完全打破。很多基层同事很有动力和激情利用AI发挥自己的聪明才智，他们有机会成为一个非常好的贡献者，但是受制于很多旧有的架构和组织。我们要对此做更大的调整，让更多有机的小团队做大事，组织更灵敏地变化。” 本文来源： 澎湃新闻 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 特斯拉拟投30亿欧元扩建德国工厂生产Cybercab，高管称2029年投产
articles.summary: 特斯拉宣布斥资30亿欧元扩建德国格伦海德超级工厂，计划于2029年启动Cybercab无人驾驶出租车生产，年产能目标最高达100万辆。 11月16日，据路透社报道，特斯拉发出声明确认上述计划，并表示 将于今年年底前提交建设许可申请，新厂房建设最快于2027年上半年启动 。 特斯拉德国超级工厂负责人André Thierig确认， Cybercab生产线预期将于2029年首次投产。 这一举措使特斯拉成为德国汽车制造业罕见的扩张者，与大众、梅赛德斯-奔驰和宝马等本土巨头持续裁员、考虑关厂的趋势形成鲜明对比。 此外，扩建将使格伦海德工厂从单一Model Y生产基地升级为多车型制造中心，并将成为特斯拉欧洲自动驾驶出行战略的核心。不过，工厂产能的就绪与Cybercab在欧洲的道路运营许可，仍是两条进展节奏各异的进程。 扩建规模：新厂房面积约为现有主车间两倍 根据特斯拉发给媒体的声明及相关报道，新生产厂房计划建在现有主厂房北侧，占地面积约50万平方米，约为现有主生产车间的两倍，相当于约70个足球场。 该设施专为Cybercab生产而设计，远期年产能目标为100万辆，但特斯拉未就达到这一水平给出具体时间表。 此次30亿欧元投资涵盖新生产厂房、配套附属建筑及新增污水处理设施。 针对当地敏感的用水问题，André Thierig承诺，即便完成扩建，工厂用水量也将维持在现有合同约定额度之内。 特斯拉已启动相关人员招募，计划在建设和生产规划阶段新增数百名员工。 若扩建完成，格伦海德工厂的产能将有望超越大众集团位于沃尔夫斯堡的总部工厂，成为德国规模最大的汽车生产基地。 现有运营：Model Y产量提升，电池投产在即 在推进扩建计划的同时，格伦海德工厂的现有业务也在持续强化。今年，特斯拉逐步推进增产，Model Y周产量已从此前约5000辆提升至目前约7000辆，下一步计划达到7500辆，接近现有设施产能上限。今年夏季，工厂新增约2000名员工，目前员工总数约为1.3万人。 不过，2025年该工厂全年生产约20.2万辆汽车，同比减少约9000辆，显示此前产能爬坡并非一帆风顺。 在新产品线方面，André Thierig介绍，工厂计划于2027年年中启动电池电芯生产，规划年产能为18吉瓦时，时间节点早于Cybercab投产计划。与此同时，特斯拉计划于2027年夏末在美国得克萨斯州奥斯汀工厂结束Cybertruck生产，以便为更多Cybercab产能腾出空间。 监管与劳工，两道绕不开的障碍 外界对此次扩建计划的关注，并不仅限于商业层面。 据报道，汽车行业分析师Matthias Schmidt在肯定这一投资对德国汽车业具有积极意义的同时提出质疑： 德国应该追问，这笔投资中有多少能够转化为可持续的长期就业，又有多少将以高度自动化、低劳动力需求的方式运转？ 工会关系方面，德国格伦海德工厂与德国强势制造业工会IG Metall长期存在摩擦。IG Metall指控特斯拉采取打压工会的策略，特斯拉则表示该工会不过是在维护自身利益。 扩建许可能否按计划推进是另一关键变量。 德国勃兰登堡州的许可审批流程历来受到严格审查，尤其涉及环境影响评估。 此次扩建并非从零开始，特斯拉此前已于2023年提交整体扩建申请，并于2024年10月获得第一阶段许可，本次新厂房申请属于后续扩建部分，仍需补充材料完成相应审批。 德国勃兰登堡州长Dietmar Woidke对这项投资表示欢迎，称其具有重大经济意义，也表明德国仍能吸引大型工业投资。 上路资格：欧洲监管框架尚未就绪 工厂投产计划明确，但Cybercab能否在欧洲大规模商业运营，仍面临显著的监管不确定性。 Cybercab是一款没有方向盘和踏板、设计用于无人驾驶状态载客的车型。 特斯拉已于今年9月在美国得克萨斯州奥斯汀启动Cybercab商业载客服务。 欧洲方面，特斯拉受监督版FSD驾驶辅助系统的审批正在推进，但覆盖范围有限。今年4月，荷兰车辆管理机构RDW批准该系统在荷兰使用，要求驾驶员保持持续监督并随时准备接管。 此后比利时、丹麦、德国等共11个欧盟成员国陆续认可荷兰审批结果，但覆盖整个欧盟的统一审批仍在欧洲汽车技术委员会审议中。 值得注意的是，受监督版FSD的辅助驾驶审批与Cybercab的完全无人驾驶商业运营许可属于不同层级的监管事项—— 前者仍依赖人类驾驶员接管，而无方向盘的Cybercab则面临更为严苛的欧洲L4级商业运营立法门槛。 因此，即便FSD在欧审批取得进展，也不意味着Cybercab能同步获准上路；格伦海德工厂的产能，或将早于欧洲无人驾驶商业监管框架而准备完毕。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 英伟达三季度缩减上市股票持仓：英特尔遭减持25%，SpaceX获增持6%
articles.summary: 英伟达正在调整其公开股票投资组合：在继续增持SpaceX的同时，大幅削减英特尔持仓。 美国证券交易委员会（SEC）披露的13F文件显示，截至2026年9月30日，英伟达持有的需申报美国上市证券共计8项，组合总市值约483.31亿美元，低于二季度末的634.4亿美元，环比下降约23.8%。 截至三季度末英伟达持有约1.305亿股SpaceX股票，高于二季度末的约1.228亿股，增幅约6%；英特尔持股则从约2.148亿股降至约1.611亿股，降幅约25%。 持仓来源：两笔投资的前因后果 英伟达持有SpaceX股份的路径颇为迂回。 2026年1月，英伟达向AI公司xAI投资100亿美元。仅一个月后，SpaceX宣布收购xAI，英伟达对xAI的直接持仓随之转化为对SpaceX的间接敞口。 2026年6月，SpaceX完成上市——业内将此次IPO描述为创纪录的事件——英伟达的间接持仓正式转变为直接持股。 英特尔持仓的来源则相对清晰。2025年12月，英伟达通过一笔50亿美元的私募定向增发取得英特尔股份，彼时对应约4%的英特尔股权。 战略逻辑：投资与客户关系的双重考量 SpaceX正快速成为英伟达AI GPU产品的重要客户，这使得这笔持股兼具财务投资与客户关系维护的双重属性。在此背景下增持，既是对SpaceX成长潜力的押注，也有助于深化双方的业务纽带。 英特尔持仓的削减信号则更为复杂。25%的减持幅度表明英伟达在重新评估这一头寸，但保留逾1.6亿股又说明其并未选择彻底退出，外界对于减持动机的解读空间依然开放。 从更宏观的视角来看，英伟达超过480亿美元的投资组合将其与AI及航天领域的客户、竞争对手和合作伙伴紧密捆绑。这一组合已足够庞大，足以作为独立议题受到市场关注，其波动对英伟达整体财务表现的影响也将与日俱增。 公开股票投资组合规模降至483亿美元 SEC文件显示，英伟达三季度13F报告共披露8项持仓，期末总市值约483.31亿美元，低于二季度末的634.4亿美元。 从披露规模看，英伟达公开股票组合的期末市值环比下降约23.8%。不过，这一变化不仅可能受到持仓买卖影响，也会受到相关股票价格波动影响，不能简单等同于英伟达净卖出了约151亿美元股票。 13F报告反映的是机构投资者在季度末的特定证券持仓，而不是季度内完整交易记录。报告无法直接说明具体交易时间、成交价格，也不涵盖全部非上市股权投资及其他资产。 总体来看，英伟达三季度投资组合呈现出一定的结构性调整：继续增加对SpaceX的股权敞口，同时显著降低对英特尔的持股。这一变化也使其公开股票投资组合中，AI产业链相关企业与SpaceX等战略投资对象之间的配置关系值得进一步关注。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 微软全球服务宕机调查：一个潜伏四个月的漏洞，15小时才发现问题所在
articles.summary: 微软一个隐藏长达四个月的系统漏洞， 在上周引发了一场波及全球的服务中断事故 ，暴露出高度依赖单一科技供应商的潜在风险。 此次事故始于11月11日的一次例行流量调配操作，直至次日上午11时30分——即美国企业流量高峰期——微软才意识到问题的严重性。 此后，公司又耗费约15小时排查故障并着手部署修复方案，导致众多企业和政府客户工作陷入停滞。在事故最严重时段，Outlook后台超过80%的服务器处于无响应状态，Teams视频会议邀请消失，员工不得不转而依赖电话和纸笔维持工作。 微软负责职场软件业务的执行副总裁Charles Lamanna周一在X平台发文，就此次宕机事件正式道歉。截至发稿，微软周一盘中下跌1.2%。 一次例行操作，引爆连锁崩溃 据微软向客户发布的初步报告，该漏洞早在今年7月便已潜伏于公司数据中心，却始终未被发现。 事故导火索是11月11日纽约时间晚8时许的一次自动流量切换操作：Teams视频会议与即时通讯服务的流量被自动转移至同时承载Outlook流量的另一组服务器。 与此同时，本周早些时候一个独立问题已造成部分服务器容量损失，双重压力之下触发了上述潜伏漏洞——服务器在流量骤增后出现内存耗尽。 问题随之迅速蔓延。 微软的自动化容灾系统将流量和邮件转移至其判断为"健康"的其他服务器，却将同一漏洞带入这些系统，形成连锁失效。 从最初出现零散故障，到微软确认全面问题，历时约15小时；公司随后又花费约15小时才开始推送修复方案。 自动化系统"帮倒忙"，修复工作一波三折 此次宕机持续时间之长，远超同类事故的通常水平——同类事故往往仅持续数小时。 微软面向使用Microsoft 365产品的技术人员发布的详细时间线显示，公司原本旨在维持服务稳定运行的自动化机制，反而加速了此次连锁崩溃。 恢复上线的服务器因积压的待处理流量蜂拥而至，再度过载失效，使修复进程陷入循环。 此外，由于该漏洞已在系统中潜伏数月，通过回滚近期更新来稳定系统的常规手段也宣告无效，进一步拖延了恢复进程。 实验室测试未能模拟真实环境 Charles Lamanna解释了漏洞得以长期潜伏、未被测试流程发现的原因。 微软在向外部大规模部署系统变更前，会先在实验室环境及小范围网络中进行测试，这是大型互联网服务公司的标准操作流程。 然而此次漏洞未能被拦截，原因在于实验室中模拟的流量模式和硬件配置，与服务器在真实环境中所遭遇的条件存在差异。 Lamanna指出， 微软的测试通常侧重于配置较旧、性能较弱的系统，以评估更新是否会拖垮整体架构中的薄弱环节。而此次导致服务器宕机的漏洞，在处理能力更强的新型硬件上破坏力反而更大——恰恰是测试所忽视的场景。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
